title: Wetlands! Wetlands! Wetlands!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore wetlands: what defines a wetland (saturated hydric soil, anaerobic conditions, hydrophytic plants), the main types (coastal salt and tidal marshes, mangroves, freshwater inland marshes, vernal pools, prairie potholes, playa lakes, swamps including bottomland hardwood and non-riverine forested swamps like Okefenokee, bogs, fens, seeps, oxbow lakes/billabongs), how plants like cattails, speckled alder, bald cypress, cordgrass and carnivorous plants cope with waterlogged soil, the historical US loss of wetlands and the role of mosquito control and drainage, their benefits (flood storage, water filtration, fisheries and bird habitat, beaver dams), and ways to help (donations, local voting, private land stewardship). The episode closes with listener mail about the SYSK 5K virtual event organized by listeners.

segments.title: Opening banter and wetlands intro
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about the episode title and credit Tom Peterman, a wetland biologist, with suggesting the topic. Dave Ruz's intro material defines a wetland as land where water is present for part of the year in the soil.

segments.title: Wetland statistics and loss in the US
segments.summary: Wetlands cover about 5 percent of US land but host 31 percent of plant species, and a third of threatened or endangered species live in them. Hosts discuss how the Lower 48 had about 220 million acres of wetlands in the 1600s, and that drainage ran at roughly 60,000 acres per year from the 1950s, with development and profit driving losses until the environmental movement of the 1970s.

segments.title: Defining wetland characteristics
segments.summary: Wetlands are permanently or periodically flooded or wet, with hydric soil dominated by anaerobic processes. Ephemeral wetlands are wet only briefly.

segments.title: Coastal wetlands: tidal marshes and mangroves
segments.summary: Tidal salt and brackish marshes sit between inland and ocean and are nutrient rich, with grass-dominated plant life. Freshwater tidal marshes are inland but still tidal, and the Great Lakes have tides too. Mangrove forests grow in coastal wetlands with trunks and roots standing above the water.

segments.title: Inland wetlands: prairie potholes, vernal pools, playa lakes
segments.summary: Inland swamps, marshes, and bogs often occur near rivers and streams. Vernal pools are seasonal depressions that hold floodwater, slow runoff, recharge groundwater, and lack fish so they support amphibians. Prairie potholes in the upper Midwest were left by glaciers and serve as stopover habitat for migrating birds. Playa lakes in deserts also attract migratory birds.

segments.title: Inland swamps and the Okefenokee
segments.summary: Josh describes canoeing the Okefenokee Swamp and staying on reserved camping decks above the water, with alligators present. Forested non-riverine swamps fill from rain or groundwater, while bottomland hardwood swamps are river-fed. Shrub swamps form buffer zones.

segments.title: Bogs, fens, and bog bodies
segments.summary: Bogs are anaerobic, nutrient poor, and very acidic from peat, with acidity similar to vinegar; cranberries and blueberries grow there. Bogs preserve bodies such as bog people; the Tollund man is mentioned. Fens are peat wetlands fed by groundwater, so they are less acidic and more nutrient rich with more diverse life.

segments.title: Other wetland types: seeps, mud flats, oxbow lakes, billabongs
segments.summary: Seeps are where spring water spills over and saturates surrounding ground. Oxbow lakes form when a river meanders away from its old channel; in Australia such lakes are called billabongs.

segments.title: Wetland hydrology
segments.summary: Wetlands differ by how water reaches them: groundwater, precipitation, or tides. Wetland hydrologists study how water enters, stays in, and leaves wetlands.

segments.title: How wetland plants survive waterlogged soil
segments.summary: Waterlogged soil lacks oxygen, so wetland plants adapt. Cattails move air through aerenchyma channels from leaves to roots. Speckled alder has lenticels that pass oxygen into wood. Cordgrass in salt marshes excretes excess salt through its leaves. Bald cypress grows knees that take in oxygen. Bog carnivorous plants like pitcher plants and Venus flytraps get nutrients from insects.

segments.title: Benefits of wetlands: flood control, filtration, and historical drainage
segments.summary: Wetlands were drained for cropland and development, and mosquito control justified filling them. Wetlands act as sponges that absorb floodwater and storm surge; an acre can hold about 1.5 million gallons. Beaver dams act as temporary wetlands. Wetlands filter sediment and pollutants, and the Congaree swamp is estimated to equal a five million dollar treatment plant.

segments.title: Wetlands as fisheries and bird habitat
segments.summary: About 75 percent of commercially harvested US fish and shellfish had some time in wetlands, and about 90 percent of recreational catch depends on wetland breeding grounds. Wetlands provide habitat and stopovers for migrating birds.

segments.title: How to help: donations, private land, local voting
segments.summary: Listeners can donate to wetland groups such as Ducks Unlimited, The Wetlands Initiative, NRDC, and Wetlands International. About 75 percent of US wetlands are privately owned. Local officials who protect wetlands, such as Atlanta's stream buffer rules, matter.

segments.title: Listener mail: SYSK 5K
segments.summary: Aaron Huey Mozelle reports on a virtual 5K organized by listeners, where participants walked or ran while listening to favorite episodes. Josh and Chuck praise the listener community.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck invites listeners to email the show, and the episode ends with the standard credits.
